newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan starts oil cleanup, communities count the cost.
newsitem.headline: Japan starts oil cleanup, communities count the cost.

text.p: Japanese government workers teamed up with local volunteers on Wednesday to begin the long and filthy job of cleaning up 100-km (60 miles) of coastline fouled by one of the worst oil spills ever to hit Japan.
They were helped by the first break in the weather since a Russian-registered tanker split in two and started leaking oil on January 2.

The Maritime Safety Agency deployed 14 ships, two planes and four helicopters to try to find patches of oil drifting towards the shore, drop detergent on it and collect it before more of it reached land.
The slicks that have already arrived along once-pristine waterfronts have damaged centuries-old fishing areas and turned the shoreline into areas of black sludge.
Elderly women ignored biting winds and stood on slippery rocks to try to remove the oil one bucket at a time even as authorities said the work may be useless.

"Until we plug the source, even if we clean the shores, the oil may keep coming back day after day... We don't even know the total volume of leaked oil," a spokesman for the Fisheries Disaster Task Force said.
Authorities said there were five major slicks heading for the coast but still had no firm idea on the total amount of oil that could wash ashore.
At first, they estimated that 3,700 tonnes (26,000 barrels) had escaped from the 26-year-old tanker when it broke apart in stormy seas in the Sea of Japan.
But they said on Tuesday that the figure appeared too low. The 13,157-tonne Nakhodka was carrying a total of 19,000 tonnes (133,000 barrels) of heavy fuel oil.
Russian authorities in Moscow said both ends of the broken tanker were now leaking oil.
Japan's worst oil spill was in 1971, when 7,200 tonnes (50,400 barrels) of oil were spilled from a tanker that ran aground near the port city of Niigata.

Oil slicks have so far hit shore along a 100 km (60-mile) stretch from Kyoto prefecture in western Japan, threatening economic and environmental disaster for communities which depend on fishing and tourism.
The area is dotted with some of Japan's most fertile fishing areas as well as small ports and tourist resorts.
In picturesque Mikuni Bay in Fukui Prefecture, local residents came out in the early morning to gaze forlornly at oil-smeared shores.
Satoshi Horii, 32, an engineer who lives near Mikuni, said it was hard to believe the extent of the damage and he was worried about whether there would be compensation.
"Who's going to pay? The Russians don't have any money so they won't help and yet they are to blame," he told Reuters.

Standing with his five-year-old son, Samu, looking out over the devastated bay, Horii said: "I've been talking to my son about pollution for the last 24 hours. I don't understand and he doesn't understand how it happened and what we can do."
In Mikuni Bay, the oil has surrounded four large flat-topped rocks which were prime spots for growing seaweed, a traditional part of the Japanese diet.
Yukiko Michinoshita, 43, whose husband is a local fisherman, said: "Everything is dead. This was the best part of the coast for abalone and all sorts of fish. They were the sweetest and the best."

Local residents used buckets and wheelbarrows to scoop oil from the shore and carry it away. They formed bucket lines 20 yards (metres) long, passing the buckets up to wheelbarrows which were then wheeled up to trucks.
Most of the volunteers were women, some of them elderly.
They ignored the bitterly cold sea wind that buffetted them as they slipped on the greasy rocks where the oil had gathered.
Government agency workers used slightly more advanced methods, with chemically treated pads to soak up the spill.
Other workers in special protective clothing stood chest-deep in oil-filled waters using hoses to pump out the oil.
